content: Dr. Ruby Dhalla, born on February 18, 1974, is a Canadian politician who has represented the Brampton—Springdale riding in the Canadian House of Commons since 2004 as a member of the Liberal Party of Canada. She, along with Nina Grewal of the British Columbia Conservative Party, became one of the first Sikh women to serve in the Canadian House of Commons. Dr. Dhalla was born in Winnipeg, Manitoba, to an immigrant family from Punjab, India. At the age of ten, she gained international attention when she wrote a letter to Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, urging a peaceful resolution to the military actions at Punjab's Golden Temple. Gandhi personally responded to her letter and referenced it during a press conference months before her assassination. Dr. Dhalla earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Biochemistry with a minor in Political Science from the University of Winnipeg in 1995. She later moved to Toronto and graduated with a Doctor of Chiropractic degree from the Canadian Memorial Chiropractic College in 1999. She co-owned a chain of chiropractic clinics in Toronto, Brampton, Mississauga, and Aurora, Ontario, with her brother Neil Dhalla. Additionally, she pursued a brief acting career, including a leading role in the Bollywood-inspired Hindi-language film Kyon? Kis Liye? shot in Hamilton, Ontario. She also placed second in the Miss India Canada pageant in 1993. Dr. Dhalla has been actively involved in politics since her youth, volunteering for Winnipeg Liberal candidate David Walker in the 1988 federal election and later becoming a prominent member of the Winnipeg Young Liberals. In 1998, she was elected as the youth representative of the party's standing committee on multiculturalism. She supported Paul Martin's bid for Liberal Party leadership in 2003. In 2004, Paul Martin designated Dr. Dhalla as the Liberal candidate for Brampton—Springdale, a decision that faced opposition from the local Liberal Party riding executive. Despite the controversy, she was elected by a comfortable margin and was appointed to the Standing Committee on Health. She played a significant role in organizing the Canada for Asia benefit concert in January 2005 to raise funds for victims of the Southeast Asia tsunami disaster and later organized relief efforts for victims of the 2005 earthquake in Pakistan. She also advocated for an accelerated foreign credential recognition process to assist recent Canadian immigrants in obtaining professional employment. Dr. Dhalla supported same-sex marriage legislation in 2005, citing the importance of equality under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. She was re-elected in 2006 and appointed as the Liberal Health Critic in the Official Opposition. She criticized the Conservative government on various issues, including changes to immigration laws and the cancellation of the national daycare plan. She also called for developed countries to invest resources in combating tuberculosis in the global south. Shortly after the election, she traveled to Punjab, India, where she advocated for stricter laws to prevent the abuse of married women. In 2009, Dr. Dhalla faced allegations of mistreatment and illegal employment of two Filipina caregivers hired to look after her mother. The caregivers claimed that their passports were improperly seized and that they were forced to perform tasks beyond their job descriptions. Dr. Dhalla denied the allegations, stating she had no involvement in the hiring or supervision of the caregivers. Her brother Neil Dhalla also denied the charges, attributing the controversy to an unscrupulous agency and the caregivers themselves. A third caregiver later came forward with similar allegations. The controversy led Dr. Dhalla to step down as the Liberal Youth and Multiculturalism Critic and call for a federal ethics investigation to clear her name. Both Dr. Dhalla and the caregivers testified before the House of Commons Immigration Committee, but the hearings failed to provide clarity on the matter. Dr. Dhalla maintained her innocence, describing the allegations as a coordinated attack on her reputation. No charges were filed, and she requested privacy for her family during the investigation. Dr. Dhalla's political career has been marked by her advocacy for multiculturalism, immigrant rights, and social justice, as well as her resilience in the face of controversies and challenges.
